primitives.name: Hahn Decomposition Theorem
primitives.verbatim_quote: 29] the sum of the two series is the convergent series Σr-1μ(En), it follows that they both converge, and, since the convergence of the series of positive terms and the series of negative terms is equivalent to absolute convergence, the proof of the theorem is complete.
primitives.symbol_and_unit_ledger: {'μ': 'signed measure on measurable space (dimensionless)', 'E_n': 'sequence of measurable sets (dimensionless)', 'Σr-1μ(En)': 'convergent series of real numbers (dimensionless)'}
primitives.assumptions: μ is a signed measure, {E_n} is a monotone sequence of measurable sets, |μ(E_n)| < ∞ for some n in decreasing case
primitives.breakdown_regime: When μ(E_n) becomes infinite or oscillatory, convergence fails

primitives.name: Sigma-Finiteness Closure
primitives.verbatim_quote: (1) The sum of two [totally] σ-finite measures is a [totally] σ-finite measure.
primitives.assumptions: Both μ₁ and μ₂ are σ-finite on the same measurable space
primitives.breakdown_regime: Failure when either measure lacks σ-finiteness

primitives.name: Measure Difference Uniqueness
primitives.verbatim_quote: (3) If a signed measure μ is the difference of two measures in two ways, μ = μ1 - μ2 and μ = ν1 - v2, then is it true that μ1 = v1 and μ2 = v2?
primitives.assumptions: μ = μ₁ − μ₂ = ν₁ − ν₂, all are defined on same measurable space
primitives.breakdown_regime: Non-uniqueness arises if μ₁ ≠ ν₁ or μ₂ ≠ ν₂

layer2.mapping: GSI verifies uniqueness of signed measure decomposition; GSE enforces consistency across alternative representations in state evolution
layer2.telemetry: Equality checks between decompositions confirm structural integrity

The core structure of signed measures relies on the decomposition into positive and negative parts, which leads to absolute convergence when both component series converge. This allows for rigorous treatment of limits involving monotone sequences of measurable sets. The Hahn decomposition theorem provides a foundational framework where any signed measure can be split into two mutually singular positive measures. In GSI, this enables Bayesian updating of signed beliefs by ensuring that each belief component remains well-defined and finite. For GSE, the theorem supports deterministic state transitions by guaranteeing that the measure of increasing/decreasing sequences behaves predictably. The sigma-finiteness property ensures that sums of such measures remain manageable within computational bounds. When dealing with differences of measures, uniqueness must hold to maintain logical coherence—otherwise, inconsistent interpretations may arise. These principles form the basis for robust inference and reasoning in both probabilistic and deterministic domains.
